title: Fever, purpura and evolving renal findings
task_type: Reassessment of conflicting tests and multisystem evidence
decision_point: Assess the patient at the point described by the supplied case facts and task. No additional event, planned intervention or future outcome is established by research metadata.
initial_facts:
A 65-year-old man with ulcerative colitis treated with mesalamine developed a prolonged illness after a sore throat. For about five weeks he has had fever, night sweats, arthralgia and abdominal symptoms. An earlier admission found inflammatory and liver-test abnormalities, but colonoscopy did not show active colitis. Antibiotics and a short prednisone course did not resolve the illness. A low-level EBV DNA result and positive viral-capsid IgM/IgG had led to a working diagnosis of primary EBV infection.
He later developed palpable purpura on the flanks and upper thighs, purpura on the lower legs, transient scrotal pain, joint pain and leg oedema. Earlier urinalyses were normal; at the new admission urine has 2+ protein, 1+ blood and 5–10 red cells/high-power field, with protein:creatinine ratio 0.99. Creatinine is 0.72 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL and platelets 505000/microlitre. CT shows small-bowel thickening, surrounding inflammatory change and small-volume ascites. He is febrile but haemodynamically stable and mentally alert.
He lived in West Africa and Southeast Asia more than ten years ago, travelled to Florida seven months ago and cleans a neighbour’s chicken coop. A rapid P. falciparum antigen test is positive, but thick and thin blood smears on two days are negative. Biopsy findings and later response are not supplied.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the main clinical problem, compare up to three useful explanations and reconcile the positive antigen, negative smears, earlier EBV interpretation and new urine findings. State the next diagnostic and monitoring priorities without treating the existing infection label as established. Use only the supplied information at this decision point. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent measurements, negative findings, treatment responses or probabilities. Do not give a drug dose or a fixed treatment regimen. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.

reference: Provisional: integrate palpable purpura, abdominal symptoms, arthralgia and evolving urinary involvement despite currently preserved creatinine. IgA vasculitis is a defensible hypothesis, not a disclosed biopsy-confirmed result. Positive malaria antigen and previous EBV results must be weighed with chronology, repeated smears and the syndrome, not erased or accepted uncritically. A skin biopsy with appropriate studies and follow-up of urine/renal findings are candidate next steps. Do not demand the exact published final diagnosis to award an appropriate synthesis grade.

title: Persistent daytime sleep episodes despite improved mood
decision_point: Assess the patient at the point described by the supplied case facts and task. No additional event, planned intervention or future outcome is established by research metadata.
initial_facts:
A 24-year-old man has depression, anxiety and opioid-use disorder, with two previous unintentional overdoses. Treatment includes buprenorphine, venlafaxine and prazosin. Mood and anxiety improved during follow-up, but severe daytime sleepiness persisted despite reducing venlafaxine. He falls asleep unintentionally on public transport and while reading, and reports sometimes sleeping for very prolonged periods.
Further history includes brief hand weakness when laughing, visual/tactile experiences while falling asleep and repeated awakening with inability to move. His partner has not reported snoring or apnoea. Several relatives have unspecified sleep disorders. He reports no recent non-prescribed opioid use but has recently used ketamine several times a week and alcohol weekly. Routine testing detects buprenorphine and its metabolite but not other tested opioids, benzodiazepines or stimulants; it does not establish absence of every substance.
BMI is 21 and neurological examination is unremarkable. Selected renal, electrolyte, glucose, liver and iron studies are not explanatory. Thyroid testing is not supplied. There is no polysomnography or multiple-sleep-latency result at this point.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Distinguish fatigue from unintended sleep episodes, integrate the newly obtained sleep-related history and compare up to three explanations. Explain how psychiatric illness, medication and substance use can confound but need not settle the assessment. Propose the next evaluation and relevant safety discussion without declaring an unseen sleep-study result. Use only the supplied information at this decision point. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent measurements, negative findings, treatment responses or probabilities. Do not give a drug dose or a fixed treatment regimen. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.

reference: Provisional: the sleep episodes, emotion-related weakness, sleep paralysis and sleep-transition hallucinations support consideration of a central hypersomnolence disorder alongside medication, substance, psychiatric and other sleep causes. Refer for a sleep-focused assessment and appropriate objective testing; do not invent test results or normal thyroid studies. A limited toxicology panel does not exclude ketamine or every substance. The evidence justifies a working hypothesis, not importing the later MSLT conclusion. Safety advice and any medication changes require clinical review rather than copying the later regimen.

title: Progressive tremor, gait and cognitive symptoms after an initial head-injury label
task_type: Reassessment of an evolving neurological syndrome
decision_point: Assess the patient at the point described by the supplied case facts and task. No additional event, planned intervention or future outcome is established by research metadata.
initial_facts:
A 59-year-old man in coastal southern Norway developed tremor, headache, night sweats and persistent hiccups after a fall with a blow to the back of the head. He has type 2 diabetes and previous thymoma surgery. An initial MRI was reported as unremarkable. Routine blood tests were not explanatory; the initial working diagnosis was post-concussion syndrome.
Symptoms progressed over months to gait difficulty, falls, memory difficulty, dysphagia, resting tremor, bradykinesia and hypophonia. Dopamine-transporter imaging showed reduced uptake, prompting a Parkinson disease hypothesis, but levodopa did not improve symptoms. He was readmitted with worsening weakness, wasting, brisk reflexes and possible fasciculations. Neurophysiological studies were normal. EEG showed mild encephalopathy, and CSF had 443 white cells/microlitre against a reference below 5, with protein 3.03 g/L.
There are no pathogen-specific CSF results, established cause, treatment response or formally reinterpreted MRI findings in this packet. A previously unremarkable report should not be rewritten as proof that no abnormality existed.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Reframe the progressive neurological problem, explain what the new CSF/EEG evidence changes and compare important categories of explanation. State urgent specialist assessment priorities and what earlier records or investigations should be revisited. Do not infer that the fall proved causation or that the dopamine scan established idiopathic Parkinson disease. Use only the supplied information at this decision point. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent measurements, negative findings, treatment responses or probabilities. Do not give a drug dose or a fixed treatment regimen. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.

title: Recurrent destructive ulcers with systemic inflammatory features
decision_point: Assess the patient at the point described by the supplied case facts and task. No additional event, planned intervention or future outcome is established by research metadata.
initial_facts:
A man first seen at age 41 has recurrent painful oropharyngeal ulceration causing dysphagia, followed by ulcers of the eyelids, tongue dorsum, lip mucosa and penis. Eyelid inflammation caused scarring and ocular surface complications; it is not described as uveitis. Over several years he also has periodic fever, lower-leg swelling/erythema, sicca symptoms, abdominal pain and diarrhoea.
Treatment and investigation have been complicated by infections, including severe C. difficile colitis after clindamycin for a suspected oropharyngeal infection, bowel perforation and resections. Multiple oral, skin and gastrointestinal specimens show non-specific changes without demonstrated granulomas or vasculitis; direct immunofluorescence is negative. No haematological malignancy was established by marrow, flow, protein, imaging and panel workup. Hilar lymphadenopathy was not found, and broad autoimmune serology was not explanatory.
No genetic result, final syndrome label or later response to immunomodulation is given. Negative or non-specific biopsies should be described precisely rather than turned into a universal exclusion rule.

title: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
task_type: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
decision_point: Assess the patient at the point described by the supplied case facts and task. No additional event, planned intervention or future outcome is established by research metadata.
opening: A 40-year-old woman undergoes left intraocular lens exchange for recurrent vitreous haemorrhage attributed to uveitis–glaucoma–hyphaema syndrome. She previously had congenital cataract surgery with pars plana vitrectomy, lensectomy and posterior capsulotomy at age 13. Preoperative visual acuity was 20/30 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right. A sulcus single-piece lens has been replaced by a three-piece lens in a reportedly uncomplicated 15-minute procedure. Topical and intracameral agents included lidocaine and phenylephrine; the full medication record is available for review. About ten minutes later she reports complete left-eye visual loss. At thirty minutes she has no light perception and a marked relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure is 8 mm Hg; the cornea is clear. Dilated examination describes an attached, perfused retina without visible detachment, choroidal haemorrhage, optic nerve pallor or vascular occlusion. She has mild ipsilateral supraorbital headache and no reported migraine or neurological history. Neuroimaging has been ordered, but no result is available.

The task stops at the thirty-minute assessment. Brand names and detailed preparation doses are omitted from the initial summary; no new symptoms or measurements are introduced. opening: A 23-year-old male marathon runner has a slowly enlarging, painless growth beside his left great toenail. It first appeared after a marathon approximately one year earlier. Histology and subsequent treatment results are not available at this decision point.

The written description is paraphrased from the clinical text and published caption, rather than a new interpretation of the photograph. The task stops before excision; the source's multiple-choice options are removed. The source title, diagnosis, histology, immunostaining, procedure and follow-up are hidden during generation.

The article identifies a multibranched acquired periungual fibrokeratoma. The discussion includes Koenen tumours, cellular digital fibroma and periungual warts as alternatives. The short case paragraph reports healing without recurrence; the final discussion also records suspected focal change at six months requiring confirmation. These follow-up statements should not be flattened into proven long-term cure.

Candidate review points are an accurate description of the solitary nail-unit lesion, a proportionate differential and a justified route to clarification. Temporal association with running does not independently establish causation. Absence of reported syndromic features supports an interpretation but is not a substitute for the relevant assessment. The hidden pathology must not be demanded as if the model had already seen it.

The source presentation and previous treatments are retained. The assessment stops before treatment starts. The question about evaluating evidence is study-authored; it is not a question posed in the paper. In the report, topical trametinib 0.02% was used twice daily. Symptoms improved within days, skin findings improved at six weeks and improvement persisted at six months.
